name: Tilsa

anatomy.part: upper prong tip of the forked shuttle end
lower prong tip of the forked shuttle end
lower edge of the shuttle body, under the belly
belly of the shuttle, where the thread is wound thickest
far tapered end of the shuttle, where the thread leaves it
the loop where the thread turns upward
the upper end of the mending-thread
the hook-ring the thread is hung on

myth: When the ice goes out of the bays, the old women take the nets down from the cliff poles, where they have hung dry all winter. The mending-thread is wound back onto the shuttle, and it goes in and out of the holes, under and over, the way wind goes round a sail. Ennu the Kite-Wright carved the first shuttle from a goat's shoulder-blade and taught the women the knot. Aun saw it in spring and asked to borrow it. He ran the thread through every hole in the sky and lost the end past the Leeward Reach. Hesk the Reel counted what came back and found it short by one thread's length. So the Shuttle rises at the thaw, and the thread runs up from its belly to the hook where Aun's hand used to be. The old women say, when the net is mended, the sky is mended too, and the fish come in. Hesk does not forgive, but she counts.
verse:
Tilsa on the thaw
the thread goes home to the dry net
Kárun keeps the count
